MA004-013----:
In Dooncarton or Glengad townland, located in a narrow strip of coastal pasture, 400m S of a rocky shoreline bordering the SE side of Broad Haven Bay. A smaller sandy estuarine bay, Sruwaddacon Bay, which opens into the E side of Broad Haven Bay, is immediately NE, beyond which Benwee Head and Knockdaff are visible on the skyline. The good pastureland ends abruptly 80m to S where land rises to rough mountainous terrain.
Indicated on the 1912 OS 6-inch map as 'Stone circle'. Level circular area (diam. 4.85m) defined by seven irregularly-shaped upright boulders, ranging in size from H 0.62m; Wth 0.33m; T 0.1m to H 1.32m; Wth 0.35m; T 0.31m. An eighth stone, at NE, has fallen and is now largely grass-covered. A fallen rectangular block, possibly an outlier, lies c. 16m to NW. There is a court tomb (MA004-012----) 120m to W.

In wet peatland, situated on a gentle W-facing slope, providing good views in all directions and overlooking the Atlantic Ocean to W.
This monument is not shown on the 1838 OS 6-inch map or on the 25-inch plan. It is depicted on the 1922 OS 6-inch edition as a circle of boulders (diam. c. 25m) and is named ‘Stone circle’. Inspected in 1997, it comprises a subtriangular area (32.2m WNW-ESE; 23.6m NNE-SSW) defined by a series of thirty stones. Seven of the stones are fully upright, six are set on edge, fifteen are irregularly-shaped boulders randomly set and the remaining four stones are low and largely peat-covered. Ground level in the enclosed area is uneven.

MA010-024----:
In Belmullet town, located on the highest point of a low hill, overlooking Trawmore Bay to SW and the inner reaches of Broadhaven Bay to NE.
This standing stone is not shown on the 1839 OS 6-inch map, but is indicated as 'Standing Stone' on the 1921 edition. According to local folklore, the original location of the stone marks the burial site of a local chieftain, who was killed in battle during a cattle raid against Munstermen.
When inspected in 1995, the stone stood upright, incorporated into a modern NW−SE field boundary on the hill, and was surrounded by pastureland. It consisted of a large slab (H 1.7m above ground; Wth 1.12; T 0.29m) set upright in the ground, with the long axis aligned NE−SW. There were several buttressing stones surrounding it at its base.
It was removed from this location during construction of a residential housing estate in 2005. The stone had already been displaced and was no longer standing upright. It was found lying on the ground close to what was thought to have been its original location. The prostrate stone (total L 3.55m) exhibited lichen and weathering on approximately half of its total length, indicating the part of the stone that originally stood above ground. According to local information, marks on the stone, about midway up its length, were scorch marks as a result of a fire which occurred at a factory located adjacent to the original location of the standing stone. As it was not possible to re-erect the stone at its original location, it was re-erected at a new location (MA010-024001-) c. 120m to WSW.
Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 28 February 2019
MA010-037001-:
Situated on natural rise of rush-covered rough pasture on N facing slope overlooking Owenduff River. Incorporated at junction of two boundaries within ancient field system (MA010-037002) which includes many upright and set stones. It is very probable that the field system post-dates the tomb and it seems likely that it may have been robbed to make the boundaries. Remains consist of the last vestiges of a megalithic tomb comprising two possible sidestones with a displaced lintel between them at N and two septal-like stones set transversely to them at S with possible jambstone beside E septal. Uprights to NE and SE of tomb structure visible in bog might be court-stones. Single cup-mark visible on upper surface of lintel.
Compiled by: Eamon Cody, Paul Walsh

Located on the S-facing slope of a terrace on an E−W ridge, in upland waterlogged blanket bog c. 100m south of the townland boundary between Keerglen and Ballykinlettragh. The Keerglen River is at the base of slope to S, and there are streams to E and W. Views to the S are extensive, with distinctive outline of Nephin Mountain visible in the distance.
Two earthfast upright boulders set c. 2m apart on a NE-SW axis. The taller boulder (H 0.70m; Wth 0.95m at base; T 0.60m) at SW is broadly trapezoidal in shape and appears to mimic the humped shape of Nephin. The smaller boulder (H at least 0.30m; W 0.40m; T 0.40m), which appears to have a more rounded profile, is deeply sunken in the bog and largely concealed by heather. No other stones or boulders are visible in the vicinity.

Located on a slight rise, in an expanse of flat, sandy coastal pasture on the S side of Lackan Bay. Overlooked to S by a low ridge that merges at NE with sand dunes. The stone stands at the junction of two field banks, one oriented ENE−WSW, the other NNW−SSE.
A tall, straight-sided, pillar-like stone (H 3.3m; 0.46m NE-SW; 0.32m NW-SE), which tapers gently at the top to a roughly triangular peak. It leans slightly to SE.
According to one tradition recorded in the 1838 OS Letters, St. Patrick erected this stone, but another tradition held that it was erected to commemorate a victory of the Irish over the Danes who fled to sea from this location (O'Flanagan 1927, 196 (102)).
Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 13 November 2018
MA015-004----:
In average coastal pasture, located on a low ridge, just to SE of the summit, overlooking Lackan Bay. Nephin Mountain is prominent on the horizon to SSW, Knocknarae in Sligo is visible to ENE, and the mountains of Donegal define the far horizon to NE.
Indicated as ‘Standing Stone’ on the 1838 and 1922 OS 6-inch maps, it consists of an upright, narrow, pillar-like stone (H 1.75m; Wth 0.23m; T 0.1m), with a flat top. The long axis is aligned roughly N-S. It stands at the E end of a low, grass-covered, stony rise (3.4m E-W; 1.6m N-S; H 0.5m).

In pasture, located on a ridge, just below and to E of the highest point, close to the break of slope where ground falls away to S, giving excellent views over the Palmerstown River estuary and Kilalla Bay. Nephin and the Nephin Beg mountain range define the far horizon to S-SW. There is a mound (MA015-025002-) 50m to SW.
This stone circle is a National Monument in State ownership (No. 389). It is indicated as ‘Cromlech’ on the 1838 OS 6-inch map where it is depicted as simple circle. It, and the adjacent mound (MA015-026002-), are indicated as ‘Cromlechs’ and are both depicted as rough circles of boulders on the 25-inch plan; on the 1922 6-inch edition the stone circle is marked with a dolmen-type symbol.
De Valera & Ó Nualláin (1964, 94) record this stone circle as follows: ‘Marked ‘cromlech’ on the O.S.6” 1837. This is the more northerly of the two monuments marked under the name ‘Cromlechs’ in Rathfran in the current edition [1922] of the map. It is a stone circle consisting of some sixteen stones five of which are now prostrate. Those remaining erect are from 0.5 m. to 1.60 m. high. The stones vary from 0.85 m to 2.00 m. in length and from .40 m. to 1.2m. in thickness. The area enclosed measures 17.00 m. (N-S) by 19.00 m. (E-W).’
An inspection in 1994 recorded the stone circle as a  circular area (19.5m E-W; 19m N-S) defined by a broad, low bank (Wth 4-5m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.4m at N, 1.1m at S) in which are set twelve upright boulders. The boulders are rounded or irregular in form, and vary in size (Circ. c. 2.5-4m) and height (0.8-1.45m). They are set at irregular intervals around the circumference of the bank, some set against the inner face, but others set in the bank. Two large prostrate stones and a number of smaller stones protrude randomly from the bank, some or all of which may be the result of field clearance. The bank is generally rather low and degraded; there are two corresponding gaps (Wth 2-2.5m) at the E and W.

MA020-002----:
In an expanse of bog, now covered by forestry plantation, located c. 15m SSW of a court tomb (MA020-001----). Two of the stones forming this row were recorded by de Valéra and Ó Nualláin (1964, 36) as follows: ‘Some 21.50 m. roughly SSW of the tomb [MA020-001----] two standing stones protrude above the surface of the bog. They are aligned roughly N-S and are set 1.10 m. apart. The more northerly is .50 m. high, .75 m. long and 30 m. thick. The second is 1.10 m. high, 1.00 m. long and .70 m. thick. Though a small hollow surrounds them they appear to be set at a considerably higher level than the orthostats of the tomb and cannot be taken as connected with it. Immediately south of them, towards the road, a depression in the bog seems to be due to quarrying, perhaps for gravel.’ (pers. comm. A. O Raw)
In Novenber 2012 two further stones were noted immediately to S of the two uprights recorded by de Valera and Ó Nualláin. The two additional stones are low, barely protruding above the ground cover of moss and pine needle detritus. They appear deeply embedded in the underlying peat, and are close to and on the same N–S alignment as the two larger stones. The four stones appear to form a stone row (Total L 5.85m) graded in height, with the tallest stone at S. The tallest stone (H 1m; 1m N-S; 0.55-0.6m E–W) is an upright stone with a pointed top and an angular, roughly lozenge-shaped cross-section. It is set 0.94m from the second stone (H 0.65m; 0.7m N–S; 0.35-0.4m E–W) which is an upright stone with a flat E face and a curving W side giving it a roughly D-shaped cross-section. The second stone is 0.4m from the third stone (H 0.2m; 0.88m N–S; 0.37m) which is a low stone, roughly D-shaped in cross-section with the flat side facing W. The fourth stone (H 0.15-0.2m; 0.4m N–S; c. 0.65m E–W), 1.3m N of the third, is engulfed in peat and barely protrudes from the ground surface. Its long axis appears to be perpendicular to that of the other three stones but it may be part of the row.
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 26 September 2012

MA021-095----:
In an expanse of forest-covered bogland, 5m to E of a forest track, just below the summit of a gradual ESE-facing slope. The surrounding terrain is now entirely obscured by trees but originally the location would have offered a broad vista defined on the skyline to E by the Ox Mountains, and to S by Nephin and the Nephin Beg range. There is a court tomb (MA021-044----) located c. 200m to ESE and another court tomb (MA020-001----) and a stone row (MA020-002----) c. 800m to SW. This standing stone was first noted by de Valéra and Ó Nualláin (1964, 37). They recorded that, when looking westward from the court tomb (MA021-044----), ‘the ground rises for about 400 yards to the head of the valley where a conspicuous standing stone, about 1.75m high, overlooks the site.’ However, following extensive afforestation of the area, the stone’s location was lost. In 2012 it was rediscovered (Pers. comm. Alan O’Raw). It consists of an upright block (H 1.75m; Wth 0.8m; T 0.4m) of banded granite, with long axis aligned NNE–SSW. The stone narrows towards the top to form an asymmetrical triangular peak, with the apex at S. A narrow seam of quartzite creates a raised white scar crossing the top of the stone and extending down the north-west face and part of the NE face. There is a step fracture (L 0.35m, D 0.04m) on the south-east face, 0.3m from the base. The stone leans gently to SE. A low, roughly rectangular red sandstone block (0.4m by 0.3m; H 0.1m) is located 0.35m to SE of the standing stone. This does not appears be deeply embedded in the ground and its proximity to the standing stone may be fortuitous. Immediately to SE, a section (max dim. c. 12m) of the natural slope has been quarried out. Approximately 6m to ENE of the stone there is a level surface spread or concentration (c. 3-4m E–W; c. 10-12m N–S) of loose stones, its exact extent and nature obscured by forest debris.
Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 13 November 2012

MA022-073----:
In pasture, located on a knoll, with extensive views over the surrounding sharply undulating terrain, and to E over the estuary of the River Moy. The Ox Mountains form the far horizon to NE–E, and Nephin and the Nephin Beg range are visible to SW.
This standing stone is not indicated on the 1838 and 1929 OS 6-inch maps. It consists of an upright, pillar-like stone (H 3.1m; max. Wth 0.6m; max. T 0.5m) with a rectangular cross section, long axis NW–SE. The stone is broadest on its upper half. It tapers slightly towards the base, but has a slight asymmetrical splay on the SE side just above ground level. At top it narrows to a roughly triangular shape with a markedly pointed central apex. In the lower half of the SW face there is a small cup-mark like depression (diam. c. 0.1m) but this seems to be a natural solution hollow. The stone now stands in a small stony hollow.
John O’Donovan recorded in the 1838 OS Letters that the stone stands on the boundary between ancient territories in the Barony of Tirawley (O’Flanagan 1927, (104-105 (54-55)). According to local information, this stone was removed from the ground, in which it was not deeply embedded, during land reclamation in the 1980’s and was subsequently re-erected at roughly the same spot.
Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 3 May 2019

MA031-055----:
In undulating, average pasture, straddling SE side of low rise. Good views to E-S
This unclassified megalithic tomb is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps. A roughly rectangular chamber or gallery (4.5-5m NW−SE; 1.8m NE−SW) is outlined by six earthfast, upright boulders and large stones. The spacing between the stones is irregularly, varying from 0.25m to 1.5m. They range in length from 1-1.7m, and in thickness from 0.3-0.5m, and stand to a relatively uniform height of 0.4-0.5m. A few smaller stones, barely protruding above ground level are evident at the SE end of the chamber. The chamber is centrally located on a low, subrectangular grass-covered platform (12.5m NW−SE; 10.8m NE−SW), which might incorporate remnants of a cairn. The platform is defined by a scarp, which is well defined at S−W (ext. H 0.8m at W; 1.5m at SE), but is low (H 0.4-0.6m) elsewhere. A large, semi-prostrate slab (L 2.2m) protrudes from the ESE edge of the platform, 2.8m from the SE end of the chamber, and 4.2m to E of that, there is a large boulder (L 2.6m; Wth 2.5m; H 0.5m) on the field surface.
Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 4 July 2018
MA031-056----:
In lowlying, level pasture, 3m S of a stream, and 120m E of the confluence of the stream with the Fiddaun River. There are good, but not extensive views of the surrounding countryside, with the Ox Mountains defining the skyline to SE.
This passage tomb not shown on the 1837-8 OS 6-inch map, but is shown on the 1922 edition. It was recorded by Herity (1974, 280) as follows: ‘On a low gravel hillock, immediately south of a stream on the west side of the Ox Mountains and 10km south of the Carrowhubbock tombs (SL1, 2), stands a ring of large boulders 21m in diameter with a boulder built chamber in the centre. To the east of the chamber are two matched stones, presumably a passage.’
Inspected in 1995, it consists of a circular, flat-topped rise or mound (diam. c. 30-35m) with broadly sloping sides (H 1.7m to S). On top of the mound, set several meters in from the edge, is a circle (diam. c. 16m) of close-set or contiguous boulders, best preserved on the SW arc. There are several gaps or breaks in the circle, the largest being to N and SE. The boulders (H 0.8-1.1m; circ. 2.5-3m) are irregular or rounded in form; some are set in the ground, others appear to merely rest on it. There are a few displaced stones on the N edge of the mound. A number of large stones protrude from a slight depression in the centre of the circle. These may be part of a chamber. A pair of matched stones (L 0.7m; H 0.4m), set 0.8m apart, stands 1m to E and may represent remnants of a passage, aligned E-W. A dense growth of gorse and brambles impeded inspection.
Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 4 July 2018

In an area of level pasture, with rising ground to W. There is a lake, named Lough Agawna on the 1838 and 1922 OS 6-inch maps, 120m to SE.
This megalithic structure is not indicated on the 1838 and 1922 OS 6-inch maps. It consists of a low, oblong mound (6m E-W; 4m N-S; H 1m) of earth and stone, with four large boulders on its perimeter.
The E end is faced with a single, large upright boulder (L 2m N-S; T 0.6-0.7m; H 0.6m), extending almost the full width of this short side. Another large upright boulder (L 1.6m E-W; T 0.8-0.9m; H 1.35m) is located 1.25m E of this, roughly mid-way along the long S side of the mound. A third upright boulder (L 1.5m E-W; T 0.65m; H 1.35m) stands against the N face of the mound, more or less in line and parallel with the boulder on the S side. A large prostrate stone (max. dim.1.2m; T 0.3m) overlies the sloping W edge of the mound. The mound is irregular in shape, narrowing somewhat at the E end, with an uneven, undulating top, and has a dilapidated appearance. An accumulation of small stones on the top appear to be the result of field clearance activities. A hawthorn and an ash tree grow from the edge of the N side towards its W end.
The mound incorporates field clearance stones on its upper surface, but it is unclear, whether its core is primarily composed of earth or stone, and whether the upright boulders are set in the ground or merely pushed against the mound.
Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 31 July 2019

The sides of the mound are highest and well defined at NW, N and NE, but the S side has a low, poorly defined slump. A row of three close-set, upright stones of roughly similar dimensions (L 0.8-1.1 NNE–SSW; Wth 0.3-0.55; H 0.3-0.6m) protrudes from the NE side; the row mirrors the long axis of the mound. A single upright stone protrudes from the centre of the mound, 2.25m to SW of the row.
Heaps of loose stones and boulders, which are piled against the mound at various points along the E, NW and N sides, appear to be the result of relatively recent field clearance activites. A small portion (4m NE–SW; 2m NW–SE) of the SSE edge of the mound has been dug away.

In an area of undulating pasture, prominently sited on a limestone knoll, which provides excellent views in all directions, with the long spine of the Ox Mountains defining the skyline at E−S, and the summit of Nephin Mountain rising in the distance to WSW. A small lake, named Lough Lauravally on the OS 6-inch maps, now largely dried up, is located 100m to NW. The knoll was sporadically quarried for limestone in the past, and there is a ruined, circular stone-built limekiln (diam. 2m) 5m to SW of the standing stone.
This standing stone is a National Monument (No. 293) in state ownership. It is not indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, but is marked as ‘Standing Stone’ on the 1922 edition. It was traditionally known as 'Legaun’ or ‘Legawn' (OPW topographical files).
It is an upright, relatively narrow, roughly rectangular-shaped granite slab (H 3.1m; max Wth 0.68m, 0.65m at base; T 0.28m), with its long axis aligned NE−SW. It has a rectangular cross-section, a fairly uniform thickness, but expands slightly in width midway up its height. At c. 0.5m below the top, there is an abrupt, almost right-angled, narrowing of the stone to a width of 0.3m, producing a distinct ‘shoulder’ on the SW side. The combined effect of the ‘shoulder’ and the impressive height gives the stone a resemblance to an imposing human figure, when viewed from certain angles.
The stone now leans to the NW, and disturbance in the past to the ground immediately surrounding the stone has left it standing on a low stony pedestal. The surface of the stone is covered by a coating of lichens.

This unclassified megalithic tomb is a National Monument (No. 293) in state care. It is not indicated on the 1838 and 1922 OS 6-inch maps, but was traditionally known as 'Dermot & Grania's Bed'. It was recorded in the early 20th-century in OPW Topographical Files as follows: ‘A slight mound and not quite complete megalithic grave, lying NW to SW and partly built into a modern stone fence in the N side. Grave about 12’ x 5’ [3.6m x 1.5m]. Right side stones remain (two at W end, four on S side, two at E end) while there are two stones 4’ x 3’ x 1’6” [1.2m x 0.9m x 0.45m] lying at 10’ [3m] to E.’
When inspected in 1996, it was evident as a stony mound (c. 4m NE−SW; 2.5m NW−SE; H 1.1m)  with one large boulder visible on the perimeter at SSW, and bordered on the NW side by a NE−SW field fence.

In pasture, located on level ground in undulating hilly terrain. There is a pronounced drop in ground level 50m to E into a depression of boggy ground. The Ox Mountains dominate the skyline at E-SE, and Nephin Mountain is visible on the far horizon to WSW.
This wedge tomb is a National Monument (no. 293) in state ownership. It is named ‘Dermot and Grania’s Bed’ on the 1838 and 19 OS 6-inch maps. It consists of a well preserved, roughly U-shaped cairn (L 6m E−W; Wth 6.5 at W; max. H 1.5m at W), oriented NE-SW, which covers a gallery or burial chamber. As is typical for wedge tombs, the cairn tapers in width and decreasing in height from the broad, flat façade towards the rear. The entrance is in the centre of the façade at SW, and is flanked by two well matched jamb stones. It opens into the short gallery (L c. 3.5m; max. Wth 1.4m; max. H 1.1m) which is faced on each side by four large upright stones or othostats. The side stones support a roof composed of two massive, overlapping capstones. An outer wall of upright stones is now largely concealed by the cairn, but some of these orthostats can be seen protruding from the cairn towards the rear of the tomb.

In pasture located on a low rise. The Ox Mountains line the horizon to E-SE and Nephin Mountain is visible to SW. There is a gentle fall of ground towards a small river, 130m to N. The townland boundary coincides with the course of the river.
Three stones of unequal size and spacing are arranged in a row (L 7.4m), on an NNE-SSW axis. The two stones at either end of the row are roughly triangular in shape, with the apex of the triangle pointing to the sky. The middle stone is broad and very slightly rounded at the top but narrows markedly at base, giving it the rough appearance of an inverted triangle with the apex set in the ground. The SSW stone (H 1.7m; Wth 0.25m at top, 1m at base) is the tallest and largest, with a gap of 4.2m between it and the middle stone (H 0.9m; Wth 1m at top, 0.5m at base; T 0.35m). The middle stone and the NNE stone (H 1m; Wth 0.1m at top, 0.6m at base; T 0.25m) and are of similar height, and set 1.4m apart.
There is a standing stone (MA040-091----) 120m to NE and a possible standing stone (MA040-111----) 80m to N, both on the flat lowlying ground bordering the river.

In pasture, located on the level top of a low rise, in an area of undulating terrain. The location provides good, though generally not extensive, views. The Ox Mountains define the skyline at NE−SE, and Nephin Mountain is a focal point on the far horizon to SW.
This wedge tomb is a National Monument in State care (no. 293). It is not indicated on the 1838 and 1922 OS 6-inch maps. OPW Topographical Files record the traditional name as 'Tober na Cloiche (Tubbernaclogha)'.
It consists of roughly oval cairn (11m NE−SW; 9.5m NW−SE; H 0.7m) of earth and stones, oriented NE−SW. The cairn is largely grass-covered, with medium to large stones and boulders protruding from the sod, and scattered loosely on top. Several large rounded boulders around the perimeter of the cairn, especially at S and W, appear to be in situ kerb stones. Some of the looser stones on top may be the result of relatively recent field clearance activity. A very large irregular-shaped boulder (c. 2m NW−SE; c. 1.8m NE−SW; H c. 0.6-0.7m) rests on top of the cairn towards its SW end. The boulder is roughly triangular in cross-section, rising to an irregular-shaped peak at top above a flat base. It serves as a capstone over a shallow hollow or void in the cairn, which is partly infilled with loose stone.

Situated close to the shore at Annagh Strand at the foot of a steep N facing slope. The remains stand immediately N of a ruined hut and are represented by a tall, gable-shaped stone (2m H) aligned E-W with two other stones (0.8m H) set immediately to the N of its W end. There is a further large stone exposed to the N and it may be a possible prostrate slab. A line of small stones immediately E of the monument may represent an attempt to convert it to a pen or other structure. The monument cannot be classified with certainty in its present condition but interpretation of the remains as the last vestiges of a megalithic tomb would not be inconsistent with the evidence. Although the gable-shaped stone suggests affinities with the portal tomb class (MacDonald 1990, 7), the tomb must remain unclassified pending further investigation.

MA044-009003-:
Located in a burial ground (MA044-009001-). The burial ground survives as a low mound (14.5m ENE-WSW; 10.2m NNW-SSE). The standing stone is located at the SW edge of the mound. It is a National Monument in State ownership (No. 423). It consists of an upright, subrectangular-shaped stone (H 1.46m; Wth 0.9m; T 0.23m), tapering to a point at top, and aligned NNE-SSW. It tilts slightly to WNW. Moran (1942, 149) recorded that the W face is divided into a number of 'diamond shaped figures by intersecting lines'. These 'lines' are natural faults in the stone. There is a cross-inscribed pillar (MA044-009002-) located a few meters to NE, at the centre of the burial ground.
Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 18 June 2018

MA048-041----:
This monument consists of the ruined remains of a court cairn. The cairn (18m E−W; 8m N−S; H 1.5m) is now subrectangular in plan, bordered on the N and E sides by straight field fences. At the NE edge of the cairn, at the angle of the present-day field fences, are remnants of a court. Six contiguous upright stones or orthostats remain in situ, forming the S arc of the court; the orthostat at the W end of the arc is the largest (L 1.16; Wth 0.5m; H 0.8m), with the other five stones decreasing in size toward the E end of the arc. Approximately 2m N of the W end of the arc, there are three large orthostats (L 1-1.5; T 0.3m; H 0.8m), two are close-set on a parallel E−W alignment, and immediately to N, the third upright is aligned N−S. These three stones may be part of the entrance to the chamber, which probably extends NW through the body of the cairn. An upright stone protruding from the cairn, 5m to W of the possible entrance stones, may be the back stone of the chamber. Within the area of the court there are two large stones lying at a slant, which may be displaced capstones, and another stone appears to be incorporated into the E-W field fence at N. The whole is engulfed in dense overgrowth.
Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 28 May 2020

MA049-160----:
In average pasture, broken by rocky outcrops, located on top of a small, low roughly oval natural rise, in the foothills of the NW-facing slopes of the Ox Mountains. Immediately to E–SE the ground rises to a low N–S ridge, broken by rock outcropping and strewn with boulders, and overshadowed by the steeper mountain slopes. Extensive views SW–NW are punctuated by distant views of the summit of Croagh Patrick to SW, and the summit of Nephin to WSW.
Irregular-shaped stone (H c. 1.35m; 0.8m NNE–SSW; 0.5m) set upright in the ground. To the E and SW the stone presents relatively flat, smooth faces but the W and NW faces are characterised by irregular indentations, giving the stone a multi-angled cross-section. The stone leans markedly to N.
Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 7 February 2020
MA052-002----:
Located in pasture, with gently rising ground to N. There is a N−S field fence immediately to W, and to W of that is an enclosure (MA052-002001-).
This unclassified megalithic tomb is not shown 1838 and 1920 OS 6-inch maps. Several upright stones, megalithic in size, are evident over an area of c. 10m NE−SW by c. 5m NW−SE. Two large close-set upright boulders are located immediately adjacent to the N−S field fence; one stone is partly incorporated into the fence; the other stone is immediately to NW. A third large upright stone is located 4m to SW of these, with a number of adjacent stones of uncertain significance. A cluster of three uprights are located 4.5m NW of the pair of large boulders: there are two close set stones on a NW−SE axis and the third stone is immediately to E of these and set perpendicular to them. The remains are too fragmentary to classify with certainty, and are partly concealed by a thicket of blackthorn.
Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 26 June 2020

In pasture, located near the E end of a low ridge overlooking Killaturly Lough c. 300m to S.
This wedge tomb is shown on the 1837 OS 6-inch map as a ‘Giant’s Grave’; it is not shown on the 1919 edition. DeValéra and Ó Nualláin (1964, 74, no. 82) recorded it as an oval-shaped mound (11m NE–SW; 8m NW–SE) partly obscured by overgrowth and used as a dump for field stones. Near the centre, part of a roof stone was exposed, resting on a possible side stones. Towards the SW end of the mound four uprights in an irregular NW–SE line appeared to represent the façade of an outer wall, and a number of other stones on the outer edge of the mound may have represented outer walling. It was subsequently destroyed during land reclamation and there is now no visible trace at ground level. A number of large stones heaped against the E-W field fence at S may be from the tomb.

Three contiguous orthostats or large upright boulders (H c. 0.5m) are visible, which form part of the W side of the gallery. The tops of three corresponding orthostats on the E side of the gallery can be glimpsed. Three roof slabs span the width of the gallery between the visible side stones. The gallery is infilled with earth to a height of 0.25m below the capstones. Stones protrude from the perimeter/edge of the cairn in an apparently random manner, but at the N–NE there is the suggestion of a kerb or outer walling.

In pasture on a very gentle W-facing slope c. 80m to the W of the foot of a N-S ridge. First recorded by Rynne in 1954 (1959, 26-7) who noted the local tradition of the site being known as a ‘Giant’s Grave’. He described a low ‘pear-shaped’ cairn (L c. 12m E-W; max. Wth c.7m; H c. 1m) of small stones, some recently added as a result of field clearance and observed ‘several large flagstones’ protruding above the cairn stones, an in situ capstone towards the W with a second possible capstone close by, on the edge of the cairn. The monument was subsequently inspected by the Megalithic Survey (de Valera and Ó Nualláin, 1964, 75: Fig. 45. Plate 33) which commented that, since Rynne’s visit, the site had been enclosed by a shallow fosse (D 0.2m; Wth 0.3-0.9m) and a low outer bank (H 0.4m; Wth 0.5-1.5m) ‘to delimit the monument which was at the time in danger of destruction’ and was ‘much obscured by the dumping of field stones’. The dumping had ‘greatly obscured the site’ and several stones noted previously by Rynne were no longer visible and only small portions of others were still exposed.
Two stones roughly aligned E-W were interpreted as representing the N side of a gallery (east stone L 0.6m; Wth 0.3m; H 0.20m; west stone L 1m; H 0.25m) and a short distance (L 0.5m) to their W, the edge of a prostrate slab, a possible capstone was visible (L 1m; min Wth 0.7m; T 0.1m). No orthostats of the south side of the gallery were visible. Roughly parallel to the line of the N side of the chamber, and c. 1m to N, four stones were thought to represent an outer-wall. The conclusion was that in its obscured condition, the site would have remained unclassifiable, however, given Rynne’s previous account, and notwithstanding difficulties in exact correlation of his details with the remains visible, the monument was accepted as a wedge tomb.
When inspected in October, 2025, the monument was found to survive but grass, fern, nettle, briar and whitethorn growth obscured most of the detail previously recorded.
This monument is subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (PO no. 7/1957).
Date of visit: 24-10-2025
Compiled by: Gearóid Conroy

In an expanse of rough, heather-covered bog, strewn with boulders and broken by rock-outcropping, located at the top of broad, relatively flat-topped knoll or rise, with extensive views in all directions. The monument is situated on a terrace on a generally E-facing slope that overlooks the small valley that opens out on the seashore at Portlea (known locally as ‘Portle’). It stands immediately inside the roadside wall on the western side of the Lighthouse Road and is only 75m from southern boundary of the townland. The surrounding field surface is uneven pasture with clear traces of former cultivation ridges, although the site of the stone itself is fairly level and up to 1m above the adjoining road. Description: It comprises a squat, rectangular block of unhewn conglomerate-like rock (L 1m × Wth 0.7m × H 1.35m max. on its north-western side), its long axis running NNE–SSW. The whole surface, including its roughly flat top, is purplish in colour and speckled with lichens. It does not appear to be deeply bedded in the ground as small exposures of bedrock are visible in the field surface immediately to NW and N. Two other amorphous blocks of similar rock type lie on the roadside verge c. 10–20m to SE, but neither are purposely set. Despite Westropp’s clear description of its location (1911a, 16–17, 19), this standing stone has been recurrently misplaced on the Ordnance Survey maps (see MA085-152----1).

MA085-008001-:
Situated amid the stark, open, hummocky topography to E of Knocknaveen (known locally as ‘Glan Hill’). The Megalithic Tomb lies in a shallow saddle between two hillocks immediately NW of a small peat basin known locally as ‘Poirtín Fuinch’. This is now largely cut away and filled with water. The site affords wide views to N over the Lough Avullin basin, while to E the Peak of Croagh Patrick is clearly visible. The tomb lies within a field system (MA085-037----) and there is a possible fulacht fia (MA085-045----) immediately to SSW.
The Megalithic Tomb comprises of a large roofless chamber surrounded by a low, bracken-covered cairn, within which traces of a court are visible at its eastern end. The chamber’s long axis (L 4.75m) runs ENE–WSW, and it varies in internal width from 1.3m at the back stone to 2.05m at the entrance. It is delimited by fourteen orthostatic slabs (H 0.1–0.6m), the largest of which is the flat-topped backstone (L 1.75m × Wth 0.4m × H 0.75m). A number of large slabs are visible directly outside the south- ern sidewall, many of them leaning against the sidewall stones: these are probably displaced corbels. The chamber interior is choked with stone debris, particularly at the eastern end. Close to mid-point and directly inside the line of the northern wall is a small, loosely set, pillar-like slab (L 0.55m × Wth 0.15 × H 0.4m). This may be a partially displaced jamb stone, hinting at the possibility that the chamber was subdivided originally. The chamber entrance (Wth 0.8m) is flanked by a pair of well-preserved jambs (H 0.75m max.). Immediately outside it to S is a large upright slab (H1.05m), one of only four set stones that indicate the presence of a court. Although widely spaced, these indicate that its southern side ran in a shallow curve and suggest that its internal dimensions were at least 4.8m E–W. The cairn survives as a low jumble of loose stone, roughly oval in plan (E–W c. 19.5m, N–S c. 13m) and up to c. 0.7m in height. It is partially overlain along its south-western edge by a tumbled but relatively modern drystone wall. A number of possible wall lines are visible within it, particularly at the eastern end. A line of seven contiguous set boulders and slabs along the north-eastern edge (H 0.4m max.) could conceivably represent the remains of a revetment, but it and the other wall lines could equally be the remnants of turf stacks (Gosling 1990, 9; 1994, 42–3; Corlett 2001, 106–107 and pl. 91).
The above description is derived from: New Survey of Clare Island. Volume 5: Archaeology. Edited by Paul Gosling, Conleth Manning and John Waddell. (Royal Irish Academy, Dublin. 2007). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated.
Date of upload: 29 November 2018

In pasture, prominently sited on top of a ridge, overlooking a broad valley to E, and affording extensive views to W where Croagh Patrick is clearly visible on the far horizon.
Not indicated on the 1838 and 1920 OS 6-inch maps. Single capstone, tilted to E, resting on an upright orthostat/side stone (long axis E–W), to S of which is a second stone, on a NNE–SSW axis, possibly a displaced side stone or end stone. The SE corner of the capstone tips downwards and appears to rest on a number of small stones protruding from the ground. The tomb is located in a slight dip or depression in the ground surface.

In pasture, on elevated ground with extensive views to NE, and good views to SW, restricted elsewhere by undulating terrain. There is a ring barrow (MA092-006) 200m to SW, a rath (MA092-008) 140m to SE, and a court tomb (MA081-033) and cist (MA081-033001) 290m to NE.
Not shown on the 1838 and 1917 OS 6-inch maps. The remains consist of a setting of three upright stones. Two parallel side stones, on a roughly ENE-WSW axis, are set 1.4m apart; the N stone is more deeply sunk in the ground and leans to N. A little to E of these two stones, is a perpendicular upright, possible an end stone, which leans slightly to NE. The interior area is gently raised, stony and grass-covered. Total length c. 3m NE−SW.

MA103-042001-:
On elevated ground immediately adjacent to the boundary between counties Mayo and Roscommon.
Unpublished NMI Topographical Files record ‘the base of two standing stones, both about 2’ x 8” [0.6m x 0.2m] in plan, which were said to have been broken up with sledge-hammers about 1920.’ They were found ‘close to and in line with another standing stone [RO032-001001-], of similar cross-section’, which is located c. 30m to NNE in Co. Roscommon (SMR file).
In the early 1990’s ‘two broken fragments of roughly shaped sandstone’ found on the margins of a quarry (diam. 25-30m; D 3m) were interpreted as possible remnants of the two standing stones. Geochemical analysis of the two stones fragments (L 0.9m and 0.96m; both: Wth 0.57m; T 0.24) indicates that while both stones are carboniferous sandstone, they are from two different sources; one fragment is from the same source as a standing stone (RO032-001001-) sited on top of a low mound  c. 30m to NE in Kiltullagh townland, Co. Roscommon. The two standing stones may have stood on top of a natural rise, remnants of which were still visible at the margin of the quarry. Fragmentary human bones (MA103-042003-) dating to 3rd to 6th century AD were found at the quarry in 1991 and may represent burials or ritual deposits associated with the standing stones (Cribin et al. 1994). Inhumed and cremated burials (RO032-001004-) were also found in association with the Roscommon standing stone (RO032-001001-) and with an adjacent ringbarrow (RO032-001002-). The inhumations may date to the early medieval period.
There is a rath (MA103-041----) 290m to SW and a medieval church (RO032-002007-) 300m to SE.
Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 23 November 2022

MA110-088----:
In pasture, converted to forestry in December 2016, located on level top of a N−S elevation on the SE shore of Lough Carra. Ground falls away gently from the N edge of the elevation for c. 140m to the lakeshore. The location provides excellent views northwards across Lough Carra, with Croagh Patrick and Nephin visible in the distance to NNW and N, respectively. The Partry Mountains define the horizon to W, and the mountains of Connemara dominate at SW. Views are restricted at NE−SE by gently rising, undulating pastureland. Limestone slab (H 1.43m; W 1.1m NNE-SSW at base; T 0.5m at NNE end, 0.28m at SSW end) set upright in the ground, with long axis aligned NNE−SSW. The slab narrow gradually from the base (Wth 1.1m NNE−SSW) to the flat top (Wth 0.65m NNE−SSW) on its long axis. A right-angled vertical fracture, which extends the full height of the stone on its WNW face, gives the stone a roughly L-shaped cross-section, and causes an abrupt narrowing at the SSW end of the stone. The surface of the stone on its sides and top is naturally rather rough and corrugated in appearance; except for the SE face which is relatively smooth. The stone tilts slightly to WNW. A shallow depression encircles the base of the stone, caused by farm stock using the stone as a scratching post.
Compiled: Jane O’Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 20 January 2017
MA110-091----:
Located on level ground on the N margins of an expanse of coniferous forestry. Ground rises to S; this wooded slope is strewn with boulders and broken by rock outcropping. A large field of flat pasture/silage stretches to N.
A roughly rectangular block of limestone (H 1.8m; 0.7m NNE−SSW; 0.35-0.4m ESE-WNW), with a rectangular cross-section, set firmly upright in the ground. At a height of 1.2m above ground level, there is a sloping ‘shoulder’ above which the stone narrows to a width of c. 0.45m on the NNE−SSW axis. The stone has a naturally rough surface, which is noticeably more corrugated on the S and E sides. It tilts now gently to E. Ivy thickly overspreads all sides of the stone, especially dense on the top and slightly sparser towards the base. A small tree stands immediately to N, its trunk growing flush against the N face of the stone.

MA112-044----:
In pasture, located at the break of slope on a N–facing slope, which falls to a flat expanse of lowlying wettish pasture. The views to SW, the direction in which the tomb faced, are not extensive, with ground rising to a low ridge in the middle distance. There is a rath (MA112-045----) 20m to SE in the same field, and cist (MA112-108----) is located 100m to SE.
This wedge tomb, which is indicated on the 1929 OS 6-inch map as 'Dolmen', was destroyed in February 2019. There is now no visible trace at ground level.
The tomb consisted of a gallery/burial chamber (L 9.5m; Wth 1.4m) defined by a double wall of upright slabs or orthostats, roofed by flat slabs. It was oriented NE–SW, with the entrance at SW, and was enclosed by remnants of a sod-covered cairn or mound (overall L c. 16m; Wth 7.5m at SW; c. 4.5m at NE) .
The attached document includes a detailed description, plan and photograph of how the tomb looked when recorded by Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin in Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume II. County Mayo, Dublin: Stationery Office, 1964 (no. 93, p. 83-84).

MA116A005001-:
In rough pasture, located on a natural rise or terrace on the lower S-facing slopes of the Partry Mountains. The location overlooks the western shores of Lough Mask, with the skyline at S−SW dominated by the dramatic ridges of Maumtrasna Mountain. This stone row consists of three close-set, earth-fast upright stones in a NE−SW row, 4m in total length. The central stone, a gneiss boulder, is noticeably larger and taller than the two rounded granite stones which flank it. The long axis of each stone mirrors that of the row as a whole.
SW stone (L 0.6m NE−SW; T 0.4m; H 0.65m): a rounded granite boulder, roughly oval or lozenge-shaped in cross-section, narrowing at top to a rough peak.
Middle stone (L 1.45m NE−SW; T 0.7m; H 1.3m): a gneiss boulder, seamed with natural cracks, relatively straight-sided, with a flattish surface on top, sloping slightly to N; roughly lozenge-shaped cross-section. It is 0.45m to NE of the SW stone.
NE stone (L 1m NE−SW; T 0.7m; H 0.75m): a rounded granite boulder, roughly oval or lozenge-shaped in cross-section. It is 0.9m NE of the middle stone.
A random scatter of small stones around the base of the row appears to be have accumulated here relatively recently.
A ringbarrow (MA116A005002-) is located 2m to E of the stone row. Another stone row (MA116A006001-) and a cairn (MA116A006002-) are located 300m to WSW.

MA116A006001-:
This monument was discovered by Michael O’Sullivan, Dooroy, Clonbur, Co. Galway, who brought Eamon Cody, NMS, to see it in 1999. Eamon did not have OS maps with him, and was unable to record a precise location. An inspection in 2017 established the exact location.
-----------------------------------------------------------
Located an area of damp, rough pasture of rushes, sedges and upland grasses, on the lower SE-facing slopes of the Partry Mountains. The location provides extensive views over the western shores of Lough Mask, with the skyline at S−SW dominated by the dramatic ridges of Maumtrasna Mountain.
This stone row consists of three close-set stones in a NNE−SSW row, 3.8m in total length.  The two outermost stones are earth-fast and upright, with their long axes mirroring that of the row as a whole. The middle stone lies prostrate on the ground surface, and at odds with the alignment of the row. All three stones appear to be gneiss, a local stone type.
SW stone (L 0.58m NNE−SSW; T 0.35-0.4m; H 0.55m): roughly oval in cross-section; the top at the N end forms a small peak.
Middle stone (L 1.15m N−S; Wth c. 0.25m; T c. 0.25m): This lies on the ground surface in a slight hollow. It appears rather angular and sharp-edged in form, differing from the more rounded shape of the two upright stones. It is 0.7m to NNE of the SW stone.
NE stone (L 0.66m NNE−SSW; T 0.36m; H 0.35m): a straight-sided, relatively flat-topped stone, sub-rectangular in cross-section. It is 1m NNE of the middle stone.
The stones in this row are low and unobtrusive, barely visible when viewed from even a relatively close distance. The original status of the prostrate stone within the row is unknown.
There is a cairn (MA116A006002-) 4.8m to S. Another stone row (MA116A005001-) and a ringbarrow (MA116A005002-) are located on an elevation 300m to ENE.

Known locally as 'Giant's Grave'. Situated in recently reclaimed pasture. Site consists of a gallery (L 4m; Wth 1.6m), orientated approximately E-W. Entrance, at E. Two segmenting jambs (H 1.05m), 0.25m apart, divide the gallery into two chambers, one to the E (L 1.5m) and one to the W (L 2.3m). Jambs supported a lintel, now displaced, resting on gallery side. Two huge orthostats, one each on the N and S sides, form most of the gallery's outline. The backstone (H 1.55m) is at the W. Cairn material, (de Valera, ÓNualláin 1964, 85), since cleared, gave the site an overall length of 15m and a width of 9m.

MA120B003----:
Located on Green Island in the NE of Lough Corrib. The stone is located toward the NW end of the island, in a small clearing which is surrounded by willow and hawthorn trees, and partly engulfed in brambles and ferns. Granitic stone slab (H 1.1m; L 1m; max T c. 0.3m), with the long axis aligned roughly E–W, set upright in the ground but leaning gently to S. The broad N face has a relatively smooth surface; the S face is slightly convex, with a rougher surface. The stone is thickest (0.3m) at its W end, is somewhat thinner in the middle (T 0.23m) and narrows sharply at its E end. The N face is pockmarked with tiny indentations or holes -these are natural features of the stone.

Located to W of a medieval church (MA123-060002-) on the NW limits of a graveyard (MA123-060003-) in the centre of an early medieval ecclesiastical enclosure (MA123-060001-). This pair of standing stones consists of two upright, irregular-shaped slabs of limestones, set 1.95m apart. The northern stone is 1.69m high and 0.2-0.4m thick; the southern stone is 1.78m high and 0.14-0.45m thick. Their function remains unknown. One possibility is that they mark an old entrance into the graveyard. According to local tradition, coffins were carried between the stones en route to burial. (Manning 1987, 45)
